My experience with updates is that they literally have caused far more problems than any virus or trojan I have ever gotten. I mean that seriously and literally, mostly because I never got a virus. "Oh he's naive," you may say, "he's probably infested with spyware right now!" Well, that might be the case, but I run virus scanners and malware scanners on this thing on a regular basis, and perhaps more importantly I run multiple live CDs of anti-virus programs on a regular basis to search for anything amiss. The only things that I see are a few pieces of adware that are embedded in a few downloaded archives I have that I turned off in the first place. Microsoft is not the only one to cause these sorts of problems - Android Lollipop nearly ruined my phone trying to get on it, and from what I've seen, it rendered a lot of expensive phones into near-useless bricks for several months after its release. Further, technical support was of no assistance - I saw forums on it and the official support reps were asking if the phone was dropped in water. The only solution was "maybe reformat the phone," which in all honesty isn't much better than the end result of a bad run-in with malware. Plus, it didn't always work, to boot, so you had an expensive phone that had been "updated" to Android BrickOS edition and had its data wiped from it, all thanks to a forced update. While it is arguable that the phone being this way is more secure, that's also from the school of thought that a dead man can't talk. Linux is also not all peaches and roses when it comes to updates, and I'm a fan of Linux.

And then you get to Windows 10, which has FORCED updates that are completely opaque. Their deliberate vagueness combined with behaviors that have been witnessed thus far makes me wonder which I have more to fear from - the malware producers, or Microsoft. And I am not entirely convinced it is the former at this point.

Software is going to have security holes for a long time to come, until we come up with some manner of incorporating things like formal proof of correctness into every day development (and that particular one may never happen, considering how hard formal proofs can be). Ultimately trade-offs have to be made. My experience is this: If you blindly trust the software company not to screw you up or over, you are setting yourself up to be screwed over or up. The anti-virus makers can be very good (some are shit, too, I will admit that) and they've caught the few problems I've had before they hit. I take the steps necessary to protect my computer without dumping on patches and hoping that I won't end up with a paperweight. Not everyone does. Truth be told, it shouldn't be like this, but it is. And I have a lot more faith in security software producers than Microsoft itself - at least the security software companies have each other to compete with, unlike Microsoft.

Bottom line: Blindly advocating for one particular solution for anything is an invitation for trouble. Many features in modern OS's count, which includes updates.
